title: The Night the Bridge Washed Away
summary: After a flash flood sweeps away part of a village's only bridge, the villagers work together to build a temporary rope-and-plank crossing so the children can still reach school.
poll: Villages should always wait for outside help instead of fixing their own damaged roads and bridges.

versions.title: The Night the Bridge Washed Away
versions.text:
One night, rain falls hard on a small village. It does not stop. By morning, the river is a flood.

Water rushes under the old bridge. The bridge goes to the road. It is the only way to school.

Crack! Part of the bridge breaks. It falls in the river. No one can cross now.

"We must fix this," says Amal's dad. He calls his neighbors for help.

The people bring rope. They bring planks too. They work all day long.

They tie the rope to two posts. They put planks on top. It is a new bridge now.

Amal helps too. She holds the rope. Her brother ties the knots.

By night, the bridge is done. It is not fancy. But it is strong.

The next day, the kids cross the bridge. They walk slow and hold on. They get to school on time.

"We did this together," says Amal's dad. The village is proud.

versions.title: The Night the Bridge Washed Away
versions.text:
One stormy night, heavy rain fell on a small village. It did not stop until morning. By then, the river was a fast flood.

The water hit the old bridge hard. The bridge was the only way into the village. It was also the only way to school.

With a loud crack, part of the bridge broke. It fell into the river. Now no one could cross.

"We have to fix this," said Amal's father. He went from house to house. He called his neighbors for help.

Soon, people came with rope and wood planks. They worked together all day. They tied thick rope between two strong posts.

Next, they laid planks across the rope. This made a path. It swayed a bit, but it held. Amal helped too. She held the rope. Her brother tied the knots.

By evening, the new crossing was ready. It was simple, but it felt safe.

The next morning, the children walked slowly across the rope bridge. They held tight to the sides. They made it to school on time.

"We built this together," said Amal's father. The village felt proud.

One stormy night, heavy rain fell on a small village near the mountains. It did not stop until morning. By then, the river had become a dangerous flood.

The rushing water hit the old wooden bridge. The bridge was the only way into the village. It was also the only route the children had to reach school. With a loud crack, part of the bridge broke away and fell into the river below.

"We have to fix this right away," said Amal's father, a farmer who had lived in the village his whole life. He went from house to house. He called on his neighbors for help.

Soon, villagers gathered with rope and wooden planks. They worked together through the morning. They tied thick rope between two sturdy posts on each side of the river.

Next, they laid planks carefully across the rope. This formed a narrow path. It swayed a little when the wind picked up, but it held firm. Amal helped too. She held the rope steady while her brother tied each knot tight.

By evening, the new rope-and-plank crossing was ready. It looked simple and plain. But it felt sturdy and safe.

The next morning, the children walked slowly across the bridge. They gripped the rope with both hands. One by one, they crossed safely and reached school right on time.

"We built this together," said Amal's father, smiling. Everyone in the village felt proud of what they had done.

versions.title: The Night the Bridge Washed Away
versions.text:
Every year, heavy rains visited the small mountain village where Amal lived. But no one expected the storm that struck one night to be so severe. Rain fell without pause from dusk until dawn. By morning, the river below the village had turned into a fast, rushing flood.

The water battered the old wooden bridge. It was the only link between the village and the main road. It was also the only footpath the children used to reach school. With a sharp crack, part of the bridge gave way and crashed into the river.

"We cannot wait for help," said Amal's father, a farmer. He went door to door, asking neighbors to help, rather than waiting for anyone else to intervene.

By midday, a crowd had gathered at the river. They carried rope and stacks of wooden planks, some salvaged from nearby sheds. Together, they set two posts on each bank and tied thick rope between them.

Next came the planks. They laid them one by one across the rope to make a footpath. It swayed with the wind, but it held firm. Amal held the rope steady while her brother tied knot after knot.

By evening, tired but pleased, the villagers stepped back. They had built a simple rope-and-plank bridge, strong enough to carry a child's weight.

The next morning, Amal and her classmates crossed the swaying bridge slowly, holding the rope tight. One by one, they reached the other side and got to school on time.

"We solved this together," Amal's father declared. The whole village agreed.

versions.title: The Night the Bridge Washed Away
versions.text:
Every year, seasonal rains visited the small mountain village where Amal lived, yet no one anticipated the severity of the storm that struck one particular night, a storm that would ultimately test the community's resourcefulness in ways no one had foreseen. Rain fell without pause from dusk until dawn, and by morning the river below the village had swollen into a fast, churning flood that frightened even the oldest residents, who had witnessed countless storms over the decades and rarely spoke of fear.

The rushing water battered the old wooden bridge, the only link between the village and the main road and the only footpath the children used each day to reach school; with a sharp crack that echoed across the valley, a section of the bridge gave way entirely and plunged into the river, leaving a gap too wide and too dangerous for anyone to attempt crossing on foot. "We cannot simply wait for outside assistance to arrive," declared Amal's father, a farmer who had crossed that very bridge nearly every day of his life and understood its importance to the village better than most, and he went from door to door, urging his neighbors to gather and confront the problem together rather than waiting for anyone to intervene from beyond the valley.

By midday, a crowd had assembled at the riverbank, carrying coils of sturdy rope and stacks of wooden planks salvaged from nearby homes and sheds; together, they planted two sturdy posts into the ground on each bank and stretched thick rope tightly between them, testing its strength repeatedly before proceeding further with the delicate work ahead. Next came the planks, laid methodically one by one across the taut rope to form a narrow footpath suspended precariously above the rushing water, a structure that swayed noticeably with each gust of wind yet held remarkably firm beneath their feet, a testament to the villagers' careful, deliberate labor. Amal held the rope steady while her older brother tied knot after knot, careful not to leave any of them loose or unevenly spaced.

By evening, exhausted but deeply satisfied, the villagers stepped back to examine what they had accomplished together: a simple rope-and-plank bridge, sturdy enough to carry a child's weight safely across the churning water below, built in a single determined day through collective effort rather than any outside intervention whatsoever.

The following morning, Amal and her classmates crossed the swaying bridge slowly, gripping the rope tightly with both hands as the river rushed beneath them, and one by one they reached the far bank and arrived at school precisely on time, relieved and visibly proud of what their village had achieved overnight. "We solved this problem together, as a single village," Amal's father declared proudly, and not a single person in the crowd disagreed with his words, since everyone understood exactly what the long night and the determined day had cost, and what, together, they had accomplished. In the years that followed, whenever Amal crossed a bridge of any kind, she remembered that night, and the quiet lesson it had taught her: that a community's greatest strength often lies not in avoiding hardship, but in facing it together, swiftly and without waiting for someone else to act.

questions.stem: What can you tell about the village from how quickly they respond to the flood?

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events in the story?

MID.prompt: Explain how the villagers worked together to solve the problem of the broken bridge. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how the villagers worked together.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The villagers worked together to solve the problem of the broken bridge. First, Amal's father went door to door asking his neighbors for help instead of waiting for outside help. Then, a crowd gathered with rope and planks salvaged from nearby homes, and together they tied the rope between two posts and laid planks across it. By working as a team, they finished a safe crossing in a single day.

A large crowd assembled outside the stadium before the game began.

keyWords.definition: saved or recovered something useful from damage or disaster

keyWords.definition: in a way that is not firmly fixed and could easily fall or fail

keyWords.definition: to step in and take action to change a situation

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?

questions.stem: According to Amal's father, why shouldn't the village simply wait for outside assistance?
options: Because outside help is forbidden by law in that region, and no one may ask for it
Because the village must solve urgent problems itself rather than waiting helplessly

Because the villagers do not trust anyone outside their village, even the nearby towns

wrong.C: The road exists; the bridge connecting to it is damaged.

questions.stem: In the passage, the word precariously most nearly means —
options: firmly and permanently fixed in place
in a way that could easily fall or fail
quickly and without any caution
brightly and in a very noticeable way

wrong.C: Precariously describes stability, not speed.
wrong.D: Precariously does not describe brightness or visibility.

questions.stem: Why does the rope-and-plank crossing sway but still hold firm?
options: Because the posts and rope were set and tied carefully, then tested for strength

Because the crossing is not actually attached to anything at either end on the riverbanks

wrong.B: The current pulls at the structure; it does not push it upward.
wrong.C: The planks are wood, not metal.
wrong.D: The crossing is tied firmly to the posts on each bank.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about the village's sense of community from how quickly the crowd assembles?
options: The villagers only help one another when a reward is offered
The villagers share a strong habit of mutual support in a crisis
The villagers rarely interact with each other outside of emergencies
The villagers are largely indifferent to one another's problems

wrong.A: No reward is mentioned as a motivation.
wrong.C: The story does not describe their interactions outside this event.
wrong.D: Their rapid, coordinated response shows the opposite of indifference.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen.
options: Amal's father gathers neighbors → the children cross → the bridge breaks → the crowd builds the crossing
The bridge breaks → Amal's father gathers neighbors → the crowd builds the crossing → the children cross
The crowd builds the crossing → the bridge breaks → the storm begins → Amal's father gathers neighbors
The children cross the new bridge → the storm begins → the bridge breaks → the crowd builds a bridge

wrong.C: The storm and the break happen before any building begins.

questions.stem: How does Amal's role in the story differ from her father's?
options: Amal refuses to help, while her father does every bit of the work alone, with the rope and the boat
Amal contributes direct physical help with the rope, while her father organizes the broader effort
Amal leads the project while her father watches from a distance and says little

wrong.A: Amal actively helps rather than refusing.
wrong.C: Her father actively organizes; he does not merely watch.
wrong.D: Their roles in the story are described somewhat differently.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by describing what Amal remembers years later about the bridge?
options: To describe in detail a different bridge in another village far away, with its builders
To criticize Amal's father for acting too quickly during the crisis in the storm, and for his anger
To explain why bridges in general are built from wood rather than from stone, in most old villages
To emphasize a lasting lesson about facing hardship together rather than waiting passively
questions.why: Ending with Amal's later reflection reinforces the story's broader theme about community resilience and acting rather than waiting.

wrong.A: No other village or bridge is introduced at the end.
wrong.B: The ending praises, rather than criticizes, her father's quick action.
wrong.C: The story never explains general bridge-building materials.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says villages should always wait for outside help instead of fixing their own damaged roads and bridges. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the flood, the crossing, and the villagers' decisions.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that villages should always wait for outside help instead of fixing problems themselves. In the story, Amal's father insists the village cannot simply wait and instead gathers his neighbors to act immediately, building a safe rope-and-plank crossing in a single day using salvaged rope and planks. This quick, collective action lets the children reach school again right away. Someone might argue that waiting for trained workers would produce a stronger, more permanent bridge, which is reasonable, but the story shows that a careful, well-tested temporary solution can still be both effective and safe when outside help might take far too long to arrive.
